### page_1
Geophys. J.R. astr. Soc (1973) 34, 435-450 
Palaeomagnetism of Precambrian Birrimian and Tarkwaian 
Rocks of West Africa 
J. D. A. Piper and Keith Lomax 
(Received 1973 April 6) 
Summary 
This paper reports the first palaeomagnetic results from Precambrian rocks 
of the West African region. Five statistically-significant sites collected 
from a greenstone body (2200 My) in the Ashanti gold mines at Obuasi, 
Ghana, give a total NRM grouping of D = 320", I = 26"(01~~ = 19"). This 
collection does not respond to a.f. cleaning, and IRM studies suggest that 
the NRM may be carried by multidomain magnetite. A dolerite dyke 
cutting the greenstone body gives a direction of magnetization D = 327" 
and I = -3"(cr,, = 11"). The grouping of five sites from basic intrusions 
in Tarkwaian rocks at Tarkwa, Ghana, is improved when they are 
corrected for the dip of the intruded sediments when they combine to 
give a mean direction of D = 156", I = 40"(01,~ = 14"). The well-grouped 
sites from this collection show high stability to a.f. demagnetization. 
Only one of five surface sites in post-orogenic dolerites in eastern Ivory 
Coast is statistically significant after a.f. cleaning and it gives a direction of 
D = 281",Z = 14" (ag5 = 39"). 
The palaeomagnetic poles (either north or south) derived from this 
study all lie in the south-central Indian ocean and are in the vicinity of 
poles of similar age from Guyana and Suriname after allowance for 
Mesozoic and later continental drift. The new West African poles, 
which refer approximately to the time interval 2200-2000 My, lie on the 
smooth continuation of the polar wander curve derived from southern 
Africa for the interval 2700-2300 My partially bridging the gap between 
that curve and the next southern African data (c. 1950 My). This suggests 
that later intercratonic movement between western and southern Africa 
has been slight, though more data are needed to confirm this. 
1. Introduction 
A major problem of pre-Mesozoic crustal tectonics concerns the development of 
the ancient orogenic belts. The widespread recognition that young orogenies have 
occurred near destructive plate margins has raised the question as to whether or not 
older orogenic belts were similarly situated. Several Phanerozoic orogenies have been 
interpreted in terms of plate tectonics (Dewey 1969; Bird & Dewey 1970) and Burke 
& Dewey (1972) have applied such an explanation to ancient orogenic belts in Africa. 
Some authors however, have argued that older orogenies were radically different 
from Phanerozoic ones (Anhausser et al. 1969; Clifford 1968). In particular the

cratonic nuclei which have not suffered thermal or orogenic events since at least 
1800 My (after Clifford 1968). 
correlation of platform sediments in shield areas with those in the orogenic belts and 
the recognition of reworked continental basement within the orogenic belts present 
major obstacles to the general application of a plate tectonic model to Precambrian 
orogenesis. 
Because other methods are inapplicable palaeomagnetism will be the principal 
method for quantifying movements of crustal plates in Palaeozoic and Precambrian 
times. As the first part of an attempt to resolve the problem of Precambrian orogenesis 
in Africa a collection has been made from Lower Proterozoic rocks of the Birrimian 
and Tarkwaian orogenic belts occupying the eastern margin of the West African 
craton. This craton is separated from the Rhodesia-Transvaal craton (Fig. 1, inset 
diagram), from which all previous palaeomagnetic collections ot comparable age have 
been obtained, by belts which have been subjected to later orogenic episodes. These 
belts are the Ubendian (> 1850 My), the Kibaran (1100k200My) and the ‘Pan 
African’ (550+ 100 My). Comparison of the southern Africa data with the new results 
enables the net relative lateral movement between the Rhodesia-Transvaal and West 
Africa cratons to be estimated. 
2. Geological outline 
The Birrimian rocks of West Africa consist predominantly of low grade metasedi- 
ments and metavolcanics and include slates, phyllites, sericite-schists and greywackes 
(Junner 1932). They are steeply folded with a predominantly NNE structural trend. 
In the Obuasi area the important gold veins of the Birrimian are closely related to a 
greenstone body within metasediments. A palaeomagnetic collection has been made 
from this body in the Ashanti gold mines. 
Downloaded from https://academic.oup.com/gji/article/34/4/435/663415 by Curtin University Library user on 29 April 2026

### page_3
Palaeomagnetism of Precambrian rocks of West Africa 437 
It has a complex geometry being elongated along the regional strike, up to 150 m 
in thickness, and becoming more subdivided with height above sea level. The ore 
lodes are believed to have been emplaced more or less contemporaneously with the 
regional metamorphism (Junner 1932) and the greenstone was entirely reconstituted 
by metasomatism associated with the mineralization. Petrographic examination shows 
the greenstone to consist of quartz, chlorite, albite, carbonate, actinolite, amphibole 
and opaques in variable amounts. The opaque minerals include large euhedral 
crystals of arsenopyrite and pyrite, minute grains of gold, and ilmenite and magnetite 
as separate phases. The magnetite varies both in quantity and form, occurring in 
some sections as aggregates of crystals, sometimes intergrown with ilmenite and some- 
times as separate, mostly euhedral crystals. It is however, uniformly fresh and 
unoxidised. 
The Obuasi greenstone has been cut by a post-orogenic dolerite dyke which has 
also been sampled for the present study, and both have been subjected to extensive 
regional shearing. This dyke is entirely fresh, it has a poikilitic texture with large 
titanaugite crystals enclosing labradorite. Considerable heavily-resorbed olivine is 
also present. The ore minerals consist of 10-20 per cent of titanomagnetite with small 
amounts (< 1 per cent) of pyrite. The titanomagnetites occur as large skeletal 
aggregates intersertal with respect to the feldspar, as aggregates pseudomorphing 
resorbed olivines, and as fine crystals within the groundmass. Some of the magnetite 
grains have up to 50 per cent of their area subdivided by dense ilmenite exsolution 
lamellae and fall in the oxidation class 2 of Ade-Hall et aZ. (1968). Post-mineralization 
faulting of these rocks is rare and confined largely to the shear zones. 
The Tarkwaian series is composed predominantly of alluvial material and appears 
to be a molasse deposit (Sestini 1971). It is separated from the underlying Birrimian 
by a minor unconformity, and the two series are folded together along similar axes 
and with intensity which decreases towards the south-west. The Tarkwaian is now 
confined to a number of elongated outcrops running NNE-SSW in Ghana and Ivory 
Coast; like the Birrimian series it is metamorphosed to middle greenschist or amphi- 
bolite facies and is considered by Sestini (1971) to be the final depositional facies of the 
Eburnean geosynclinal cycle. The Tarkwaian contains banket gold which is generally 
considered (Junner, Hirst & Service 1942; Sestini 1970) to be sedimentary in origin but 
in the Tarkwaian region the palaeocurrent directions are such as to preclude a direct 
derivation from known gold bearing veins in the Birrimian. The type outcrop of the 
Tarkwaian is extensively cut by dykes and sills of dolerite (sampled during this study) 
and microgranite. The dolerites show varying degrees of metamorphism up to green- 
schist facies and were evidently intruded at about the same time as, or shortly after, 
the regional metamorphism. They were probably intruded before the folding (Junner 
et aZ. 1942) and like the Ashanti greenstone have been subject to later shearing. 
The intrusions sampled for this study are fine to medium grained quartz dolerites 
with laths of largely fresh augite set in a matrix of quartz and plagioclase feldspar. 
Some secondary quartz and feldspar are also present. The opaque minerals comprise 
predominantly titanomagnetite which occurs both as long needle-like crystals and 
partially resorbed skeletal grains. There is no optically-detectable subdivision of 
the titanomagnetite grains by ilmenite lamellae, but there is an incipient alteration of 
some grains to haematite. 
Unmetamorphosed post-Birrimian dolerites outcrop in several parts of Ghana 
and Ivory Coast and evidently represent several intervals of intrusion (Knopf 1967). 
These dolerites have been sampled in the east of Ivory Coast near Aboisso where one 
K-Ar age of 1730+170My has been reported (Knopf 1967). They are coarse- 
grained intrusions containing hornblende, albite plagioclase which is locally sericitized, 
and quartz. The only visible opaques are large resorbed crystals of titanomagnetite 
with re-entrants. These grains are entirely fresh and show no visible oxidation. 
The age of the Birrimian and Tarkwaian igneous and metamorphic episodes is well 
Downloaded from https://academic.oup.com/gji/article/34/4/435/663415 by Curtin University Library user on 29 April 2026

### page_4
438 J. D. A. Piper and K. Lomax 
established. A minimum age for the Tarkwaian is given by a cross cutting pegmatite 
near Konongo, Ghana, of - 1700 My (Holmes & Cahen 1957); Bonhomme (1962) 
found that syntectonic granites in Ivory Coast marking the final stages of the Eburnian 
folding and metamorphism produced ages between 1830 and 2030 My. Later work, 
however, has suggested that these ages are probably too young and Tugarinov (1967) 
has obtained K-Ar ages between 2070 and 2190 My from granodiorites intruding 
Birrimian rocks. U-Pb age determinations on galenas from the mineral veins associated 
with Birrimian granites in Ivory Coast, Upper Volta and Guinea are highly concor- 
dant: they vary between 21 50 and 2200 My and indicate a preferred age of 21 90 f 30 My 
for the gold mineralization associated with the granites (Haughton 1963). In addition 
Dr. P. G. Coomer (private communication) has obtained a U-Pb age of 2200My 
from galena in the greenstone body of Ashanti and this is accepted here as the probable 
age of the metasomatism of this body. From geological considerations the dolerite 
intrusions in the Tarkwaian are inferred to be slightly younger than this. 
3. Field and laboratory methods 
Owing to the very heavy vegetation cover and high degree of tropical weathering 
the possibilities of surface sampling for palaeomagnetic studies in this area are very 
limited. Surface weathering effects are observed to reach several hundred feet below 
the surface and as a result the bulk of the collecting for this study was made at depth 
within the gold mines of Ghana. 
The procedure followed while sampling underground in the Ashanti gold mines 
was to collect and orient with magnetic compass one or two samples at each of several 
levels below one another, at points within the greenstone body accessible from each 
mine shaft. The samples from the different levels (each level is separated by about 
100 ft) from each vertical sample in the mine were then combined to form a single 
site. Each site thus samples a considerable thickness of the body and although they 
will not represent a spot record of the magnetic field, it was felt that this was the best 
way of averaging out local geological effects and errors in strike determinations by 
magnetic objects in the mine. In many cases it was possible to confirm magnetic strike 
readings by sighting along levels and cross cuts. The distribution of the six sites 
within the Ashanti gold mines is as follows: site 6: Spears shaft, levels 35-43; site 7: 
South shaft, levels 38-43; sites 8 and 10: West shaft, levels 21-25; site 9: West shaft, 
levels 32-33; site 11: Ayeinm Mainshaft, levels 12-16, and site 12: Justice's mine, 
levels 5-8 (level 9 is approximately 50 ft above sea level). 
Of the sites in dolerites from the Tarkwa goldfield which show a grouping of 
magnetic directions significant at the 95 per cent confidence level, site 17 was taken 
from the east limb and sites 18, 19 and 26 were taken from the west limb of the folded 
western gold reef. Site 25 is from a dyke on the west limb; all the other sites are from 
sills. The remaining sites, whose remanence is not significant after a.f. cleaning (18) 
are listed here and will not be considered further. Sites 15 and 16 were respectively 
from the east west limbs of the west reef; site 20 at Nsuta manganese mine (1.95" W, 
5.25" N,) near Tarkwa, and sites 21 and 22 from surface exposure north of Tarkwa 
1-90" W, 5.45" N were drilled using a portable two-stroke motor (Doell & Cox 1967). 
Two sites were also sampled from haematite-bearing conglomerates in the Tarkwaian 
but these proved to be too hard for cutting. 
The Ivory Coast dolerite samples of sites 1-5 were drilled from surface exposures 
and the single significant result was obtained at site 4 15 km north of Aboisso at 
3-20" W, 5.50" N. Sites 1-3 were sampled at 3.25" W, 5.35" N and site 5 was obtained 
at 3.2" W, 5.5" N.

The lump samples from the mines were cored in the laboratory to obtain 1" 
diameter cylinders for magnetic measurements, and polished and thin sections 
were made from representative samples from most sites. The directions of magneti- 
zation of the samples have been measured before and after a.f. demagnetization 
using a PAR SM-2D spinner magnetometer. One or two pilot samples from each 
site were progressively demagnetized in a.f. fields up to 1600 Oe (peak) and an 
optimum field for the demagnetization of the remaining members determined from 
the behaviour of the pilot using Briden's (1972) Stability Index. Where an optimum 
field was not clearly apparent from the pilot samples, the other samples from the site 
were measured after treatment in several increasing alternating fields. The low field 
susceptibilities were determined using an a.c. bridge system, and bulk coercivity has 
been determined for selected specimens by subjecting them to high direct fields. 
Saturation IRM's have also been imposed on several specimens followed by progressive 
demagnetization to compare IRM and NRM demagnetization curves. The pilot 
samples from the Obuasi greenstone body were heated to 700°C and cooled in an 
ambient field of 0.42 Oe for the comparison of TRM and NRM demagnetization curves.

4. Palaeomagnetic results 
4.1. Obuasi greenstone body 
Samples from this body have total NRM intensities (M,) between 8.0 x lo-’ and 
3.5 x Gauss (74 samples). Volume 
susceptibilities (x) vary between 2-3 x lob4 and 3-5 x lo-’ Gauss/Oersted with a 
logarithmic mean of 3.8 x (86 samples). The Koenigsberger ratios (M,/x) are 
low for igneous or metamorphic rocks and range from O.OOO1 to 0.6 with the bulk 
of the values lying withn the range 0.01-0.1. Irving (1964, page 93) observes that 
material with M,/k ratios in this range generally behave in an unstable fashion on 
demagnetization and this observation is confirmed by the present collection. Five 
of the six sites show total NRM groupings statistically significant at the 95 per cent 
confidence level (Fig. 6, Irving 1964, page 64). Behaviour of pilot specimens with 
progressive a.f. demagnetization is erratic (Fig. 2(a), Fig. 3(a) and (b)). There is 
typically a moderate fall in the moment at initial stages of demagnetization (up to 
150 Oe) followed by fluctuations with no systematic fall in the moment. The stability

index is of little help in isolating a suitable cleaning field; the pilot sample from site 11 
(Fig. 3(a)) was most stable at around 700 Oe at which it had a direction near D = 220", 
Z = - 35", however, this was not confirmed by the remainder of the samples from this 
site which gave scattered directions on demagnetizing in this field (Figs 6 and 7). 
A.f. cleaning is not successful in improving either within site or overall site 
grouping, and the best grouping of the five significant sites from the greenstone 
body is obtained at the total NRM level when they combine to give a mean direction 
of D = 320", Z = 26" (ag5 = 19'). This direction is removed from the present Earth's 
field and from other Phanerozoic directions for Africa and merits consideration 
as a possible Precambrian palaeomagnetic direction. The possibility of a stable NRM 
and low coercivity might arise if the remanence carrier is multidomain magnetite 
(Nagata 1961) but this is difficult to demonstrate in practice. 
When laboratory TRMs are imposed on those samples (Fig. 5) they acquire a 
moment which is one to two orders of magnitude greater than the total NRM. The 
TRMs also show an approximately exponential fall in their moments with demagneti- 
zation which in nearly all cases is more dramatic than the NRM, and is commensurate 
with their being held by a range of domain sizes (Stacey 1963). This cannot be used to 
infer much about the carrier of the original NRM since all the specimens were observed 
to undergo an oxidation on heating and it may be expected that single domain material 
was generated during the experiment. The demagnetization characteristics do however, 
exclude members of the ilmenite-haematite series as possible carriers (Nagata 1967). 
According to Lowrie & Fuller (1971) in the first stages of a.f. demagnetization the 
saturation IRM is relatively less hard than the weak field TRM for single domain 
magnetite and relatively more hard for multidomain carriers, although none of the 
natural material tested by these authors showed true multidomain behaviour. We 
have undertaken IRM studies to shed more light on the possible carrier of the 
remanence in the greenstone body. The hysteresis characteristics of the present 
samples show that they have low bulk coercivities. (Fig. 4(a).) Three specimens 
have also been given saturation IRMs and demagnetized progressively in fields up to 
300 Oe for comparison with the NRM demagnetization curves. The saturation IRMs 
of all three were systematically more resistant to a.f. demagnetization than the 
NRMs up to 200-300 Oe. (Fig. 4(c)). Zf the NRM of these samples is a TRM, the 
criterion of Lowrie & Fuller suggests that the bulk of the magnetism is carried by 
magnetite in the multidomain state. Since the three test specimens were among the 
more stable of the collection, this conclusion may apply with greater force to the less 
stable samples.

body and (b) sample from dolerite intrusion at Tarkwa. Comparison of saturation 
IRM and NRM demagnetization curves for (c) sample from site 12 and (d) sample 
from site 15.

There is currently considerable dispute as to whether the TRM of multidomain 
grains resides in restricted regions displaying properties expected of single domains 
(Verhoogen 1959) or whether it can be satisfactorily accounted for by multidomain 
theory (Stacey 1963). The magnetic properties of the Obuasi greenstone suggests 
that the remanence is dominated by multidomain carriers, and petrographic observa- 
tion shows that these must be unoxidized magnetite. This is associated with ilmenite 
as a separate phase and the mineralogy of the rock demonstrates that it has a low 
temperature metasomatic origin. Crystallizing slowly under such conditions the 
magnetite may owe its small and unstable TRM to the absence of dislocations in the 
crystal lattice (Verhoogen 1959). 
4.2. Basic intrusions in Tarkwaian rocks 
The basic intrusions from Tarkwa have intensities of magnetization varying between 
7.0 x lo-' and 9.0 x Gauss, with a log mean of 7.0 x lo-' Gauss (70 samples), 
and volume susceptibilities between 7.0 x lo-' and 4.5 x Gauss/Oersted with a 
log-mean kalue of 1.0~ (76 samples). M,/x values lie between 0.002 and 2.7 
with the bulk of the values being in the range 0.01-0.5. Eight of the eleven sites from 
the intrusions gave mean directions of magnetization statistically significant at the 
total NRM level, and five of these sites (17, 18, 19, 25, 26) give coherently grouped 
means. They are highly stable against a.f. demagnetization with high stability indices 
which tend to fall with increasing applied field (Fig. 2(d) and 3(e)). Some plots (e.g. 
site 19, Fig. 2 (d)) showed an initial increase in magnetic intensity with progressive 
demagnetization at lowfields (up to -400 Oe) before decreasing in higher fields; 
this may be due to selective removal of soft components parallel to the present 
geomagnetic field with a declination removed about 140" from the stable direction of 
magnetization (Fig. 3(e)). The remaining sites, including three sites with significant 
NRM groupings are unstable on demagnetization (e.g. site 15, Figs 2(d) and 3(e)) 
with a rapid decrease in intensity and low stability indices showing no obvious 
optimum demagnetizing fields. Some samples from the surface sites 21 and 22 show 
evidence of large soft components of NRM probably acquired by lightning strikes.

in the Obuasi Greenstone body (star is the mean direction), (b) samples from site 9 
in dolerite dyke at Obuasi, (c) all significant sites from dolerite intrusions at Tarkwa,

In Table 1 an overall mean direction of stable remanence is estimated, for the five 
stable sites. The precision estimates (k) of sites 19 and 25 are slightly lower after 
cleaning than at the total NRM level but the directions of magnetization are not 
appreciably different. Site 17 behaves in a stable fashion on demagnetizing and has a 
similar declination to the remainder of the sites but an anomalous inclination. Since 
this site is the only statistically significant one from the east limb of the gold-bearing 
reef it is pertinent to enquire whether a correction for the dip of the sediments may 
bring it more closely in line with the directions from the other four sites. The 
geological evidence (Junner et al. 1942) favours the sills having been intruded before 
the folding and if the sporadic low grade metamorphism has not caused remagnetiza- 
tion, this is likely to predate the folding. Unfortunately the local dip correction is 
often difficult to measure precisely because of large scale cross bedding in the sediments

and the folding is unlikely to have been simply concentric. Correction for the best 
estimate of the local dips brings the inclination of site 17 close to the corrected inclina- 
tions of sites 18, 19, 25 and 26, but the scatter of declinations of these latter four sites 
is increased though the overall precision is increased from k = 14.2 to k = 32.0. 
(Table 1.) 
However, since this scatter of declinations is sensitive to correction for the direction 
of dip (Fig. 8, the local fold axes trend NNE-SSW) it may be that this increased 
scatter results from a plunge component which the available information cannot 
correct for, and the dip corrected mean direction is preferred. The derived pole 
position is moved from 17" E, 53" S to 36" E, 53" S which brings it closer to the pole 
derived from the Obuasi greenstone body. IRM studies on samples from the 
unstable sites 15 and 21 (Fig. 4(b) and (d)) show characteristics similar to those found 
from the greenstone. Like the Obuasi greenstone material coercivities of these unstable 
sites are fairly low and the IRMs prove to be magnetically harder than the NRMs 
in low demagnetizing fields up to 100-200Oe. A satisfactory explanation of the 
remanence in the stable sites can be sought in terms of acicular needles of titano- 
magnetite present in these rocks, which can possess high coercivities (Morrish & Yu 
1955), and may have shapes such that they can act as single domain grains (Evans, 
McElhinny & Gifford 1968).

demagnetizing in fields of 50 Oe at which ten specimens from six samples combine to 
give a mean direction (Fig. 7) of D = 328", I = - 11" (a95 = 1 lo). As mentioned 
previously this dyke shows evidence of high temperature oxidation with the production 
of grains capable of behaving as single domains (Strangway, Larson & Goldstein 
1968). 
4.4. Dolerite intrusions, Ivory Coast 
Thirty-four samples were obtained from five sites in these intrusions. The grouping 
of NRM measurements is poor but just significant in three sites. One sample from 
each site (two from site 4) was progressively demagnetized up to 900 Oe. The intensities 
dropped rapidly and fluctuated with further demagnetization except in the case of site 4 
and 5 where a smoother and more regular fall in intensity took place. After demagneti- 
zation of the sites at optimum fields only site 4 remained significantly grouped (Figs 6 
and 7). The best grouping was achieved after demagnetizing in 600 Oe when the mean 
direction of magnetization was D = 281", I = 14" (10 samples, ag5 = 39"). 
Petrographic examination shows that the titanomagnetite in the dolerite intrusions 
from Ivory Coast is clearly magmatic in origin but no deuteric oxidation has been 
detected, and this probably accounts for the low stability of this collection. 
5. Discussion 
The palaeomagnetic poles from this study are shown in Fig. 9 where they are 
numbered in probable sequence of age. 
Pole 2 from the Tarkwa intrusions is regarded as slightly younger than Pole 1 
from the Obuasi greenstone because these intrusions inject Tarkwaian rocks whose 
formation is associated with the last stages of the Eburnean orogeny (Sestini 1970) and

Palaeomagnetism of Precambrian rocks of West Africa

FIG. 9. Pole positions from Africa known or believed to belong to the interval 
2300-1900My Ve is the pole from the Ventersdorp lavas of South Africa 
(-2300 My), Vr is the pole from the Vredefort ring complex of South Africa 
(1970 My) and Buis the pole from the Bushveld complex (1950 My) also from 
South Africa. Poles 1-4 are those derived from the present study in order of 
probable age: one is from the greenstone body at Obuasi (-2200 My), two is from 
the dolerite intrusions at Tarkwa (also near 2200 My), three is from the dolerite 
dyke at Obuasi, and four is from a dolerite intrusion north of Aboisso, Ivory 
Coast (-1740 My). A, B, C and D are poles of comparable age from South 
America after correction for post-Palaeozoic continental drift and using the fit of 
the continents around the Atlantic of Bullard et al. (1965). A and B are from the 
Roraima dolerites of Guyana and C and D are from dolerites in Suriname. Open 
symbols are anti-poles and closed symbols are poles. 
447 
which contain detrital gold almost certainly derived from mineralized Birrimian rocks 
similar to those from which Pole 1 was obtained. Pole 2 is derived from rocks involved 
in the Eburnean folding which are locally metamorphosed, and which are clearly 
older than the dolerite dyke at Obuasi which gives rise to Pole 3 but which, however, 
is affected by the extensive regional shearing possibly representing the last stages of this 
orogeny. The Birrimian folding and metamorphism define an older limit for the age 
of pole 4 from post-orogenic dolerites, and the single available K-Ar age of 
1740 170 My (Knopf 1967) must be regarded as a minimum age for this pole. 
Since poles 3 and 4 are based on single sites only and there is a large error associated 
with the latter they do not by themselves justify a detailed interpretation. The poles 
or antipoles of this study all lie in the south-central Indian Ocean and only pole 3 
(which is close to Permo-Carboniferous poles) is known to lie on the African polar 
wander curve for subsequent time although there are gaps in the record for later parts 
of the Precambrian. They merit comparison with poles of similar age from South 
America, and the poles concerned are shown in Fig. 9 after closing the South Atlantic 
to allow for Mesozoic and later continental drift (Bullard, Everett & Smith 1965). 
Poles A and B are from Roraima dolerites 01 Guyana and Venezuela (Hargraves 1968) 
and poles C and D are from dolerites in Suriname (Veldkamp, Mulder:& Zijderveld 
1971). These poles have a maximum age defined by the Guyana craton which has a 
Downloaded from https://academic.oup.com/gji/article/34/4/435/663415 by Curtin University Library user on 29 April 2026

### page_14
448 J. D. A. Piper nnd K. Lomax 
chronology and structural trends closely matching the West African shield after 
correction for drift (Tugarinov 1967). The available K-Ar and Rb-Sr data suggest 
that the dolerites from which these poles were derived have minimum ages in the range 
1550-1750 My, but there is evidence that the actual ages are nearer 2070 My 
(McDougall & Compston 1963), or even 2090 My (McElhinny 1969). As dolerites 
intruded shortly after the 2200 My structural and metamorphic event of the Guyana- 
West African cratons they merit closest comparison with the pole 4 from comparable 
material from Ivory Coast and are slightly younger in age than poles 1-3. Taken 
together the results suggest that the Guyana-West African craton lay in low latitudes 
at 2200-2100 My and that there was a latitudinal migration of the pole of 40"-60" 
with respect to present geographical co-ordinates during this interval. 
It is more difficult to interpret these poles in relation to results from southern 
Africa because information is currently incomplete for the interval in question. 
McElhinny ef al. (1968) have shown that the Precambrian results from the southern 
African area for the interval 2700-2300 My trace out an eastward migration of the 
pole during this interval so that it lay south of Africa at about 2300 My (Vcntersdorp 
lava pole Ve, Fig. 8). This migration path can logically be continued via all the 
West Africa and South American poles to the North African region in which lie 
poles from the Bushveld complex (1950 My, pole Bu in Fig. 9, Gougli & van Niekerk 
1959) and the Vredefort ring structure (1970 My, pole Vr in Fig. 9, Hargraves 1970). 
Because of uncertainties in relative ages of magnetization it is not yet however proven 
that this path is a simple one, and data is needed from southern Africa for the interval 
2200-2000 My to test whether there has been significant relative movement between 
the Rhodesia-Transvaal and West Africa cratons since this interval.
